description: In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen discovered an invisible radiation that passes straight through matter. Within months, medicine saw a revolution in it.

hero.hook: A hand, a few bones, a photograph. Medicine would never be blind again.

blocks.text: On **8 November 1895**, in Würzburg, Germany, the physicist **Wilhelm Röntgen** noticed a screen glowing even though no visible light was reaching it. Something invisible was crossing the room.
He called it **X-rays**, the “X” standing for “unknown.” Within weeks he had photographed the bones of his wife's hand. Radiology was born.

Röntgen worked with a tube in which electrons strike a target. He had wrapped the tube in black cardboard. A fluorescent screen some distance away glowed all the same. He understood that an invisible radiation was escaping from the tube.

blocks.caption: The famous image: the bones of a hand and a wedding ring

blocks.text: Röntgen never took out a patent on X-rays. He wanted all of science to be free to use them.

blocks.caption: Doctors and armies took up X-rays almost at once

blocks.text: Until then, “seeing” a fracture or a bullet usually meant cutting the patient open. X-rays gave an image of the inside without a single incision. Hospitals and armies adopted the technique at a furious pace.
At the start, nobody knew the risks. Operators ran X-ray sessions for hours at a time. Burns appeared, then cancers. It took years to accept that X-rays are powerful and dangerous at once.
Today both patients and medical staff are protected: limited doses, lead aprons, strict controls.
X-rays opened the way to all of modern imaging: medical scanners, industrial inspection, and even the study of crystal structure, which later proved decisive for DNA.
In **1895**, Röntgen discovered X-rays, an invisible radiation that passes through matter. Medicine gained a new kind of sight, provided it learned to control the risks.
